# The Data-Generating Process {#sec-dgp}

A model is trained on the examples someone collected, and then used on the examples the world
produces. When the two match, the gap between them is ordinary sampling noise, and more data
closes it. When they do not match, more data makes the model more confident about the wrong
thing. Every technique in this book is a deliberate change to what the model sees. This chapter
is about the changes nobody chose: the ones made by how the data was gathered.

## The problem

There are two distributions in every learning problem. The **target distribution** $p(x, y)$
describes the cases the model will face once deployed. The **training distribution**
$q(x, y)$ describes the cases it was fit on. A model fit by minimizing average loss on a sample
from $q$ estimates the minimizer of the risk under $q$. What we want is the risk under $p$:

$$
R(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{(x, y) \sim p}\big[\ell(y, f_\theta(x))\big].
$$

The question of this chapter is: when $q$ differs from $p$ because of how examples were
collected, which part of what the model learns changes, and which part survives?

## Assumptions

1. **The world produces examples from a fixed $p$.** If $p$ itself moves over time, that is
   distribution shift, the subject of
   [Distribution Shift](10-distribution-shift.qmd#sec-shift).
2. **Collection keeps or drops each example with a probability $s(x, y)$** that may depend on
   the input, the target, or both. If several examples are kept or dropped together (a whole
   hospital, a whole user), examples are no longer independent; the selection rule then acts
   on clusters, and the variance calculations below understate the noise.
3. **For the regression results, the model family contains $p(y \mid x)$'s conditional mean.**
   If the model is misspecified, even selection on $x$ changes which approximation is best,
   because it changes where the loss is averaged.

## Derivation or demonstration

Suppose an example drawn from $p$ is kept with probability $s(x, y)$. Then the kept examples
follow

$$
q(x, y) = \frac{s(x, y)\, p(x, y)}{\mathbb{E}_p[s(x, y)]},
\qquad
q(y \mid x) = \frac{s(x, y)\, p(y \mid x)}{\int s(x, y')\, p(y' \mid x)\, dy'} .
$$

If $s$ depends on $x$ only, it factors out of the integral and cancels:

::: {.callout-note title="Result: selection on inputs versus selection on targets"}
If examples are selected with a probability that depends only on the input, the conditional
distribution survives, $q(y \mid x) = p(y \mid x)$, and only the input distribution changes:
$q(x) \propto s(x)\, p(x)$. If the probability depends on the target, $q(y \mid x)$ differs from
$p(y \mid x)$, and no amount of data from $q$ recovers it unless the selection probability
$s(x, y)$ itself is known.
:::

This is a mathematical fact, and it splits selection into two very different cases. Selection
on $x$ changes the sampling distribution $q$ over inputs: one of the four levers, and a lever
that reweighting can undo when $p(x)/q(x)$ is known
([Sampling and Weighting](08-sampling-and-weighting.qmd#sec-sampling)). Selection on $y$
changes what each input appears to say about its target, which is the same damage as corrupting
labels.

**Demonstration on T1.** The tabular testbed
([The Testbeds](../appendix-testbeds.qmd#sec-testbed-t1)) draws $\log y = a + b^\top z +
\varepsilon$ with $b_1 = 0.8$, three correlated features, and $\mathbb{E}[\log y] = a = 1$. Each
of 200 seeds draws 4,000 examples and keeps them in one of three ways:

- at random, half of them ($q = p$);
- with probability $\sigma(2 z_1)$, so large $z_1$ is over-represented (selection on $x$);
- with probability $\sigma\big({-2}(\log y - \operatorname{median} \log y)\big)$, so large
  targets are under-represented, as when high values are less often recorded (selection on $y$).

A linear regression of $\log y$ on $z$ is then fit to the kept examples. Averaged over the 200
seeds, the coefficient on $z_1$ is 0.802 under random selection and 0.801 under selection on
$x$: both are unbiased, as the result predicts. Under selection on $y$ it is 0.670, a bias of
about nine times the seed-to-seed standard deviation. The sample mean of $\log y$ tells the
opposite story. It is 1.00 under random selection, 1.45 under selection on $x$ and 0.33 under
selection on $y$. Selection on $x$ leaves the regression intact but biases any summary of the
population (checked by `tests/test_selection.py::test_selection_on_x_keeps_the_conditional_selection_on_y_biases_it`).

When $s(x, y)$ is known, as it is in the testbed, even selection on $y$ can be undone. Since
$p \propto q / s$, weighting each kept example by $1/s(x, y)$ restores the regression under
$p$. It does so slowly, because the rarest kept examples get the largest weights. The weighted
coefficient was 0.781 with 4,000 examples per seed and 0.801 with 256,000, as the largest
weight grew from about 60 to about 480
(`tests/test_selection.py::test_known_selection_probabilities_undo_selection_on_y`). Real
selection probabilities are almost never known, which is why the result box speaks of data
from $q$ alone.

**Sampling designs.** Some ways of drawing $q$ are deliberate
[@cetinkayarundel2024ims, §2.1.5]:

- a **simple random sample** gives each case an equal chance of inclusion, with no case's
  inclusion informative about another's;
- a **stratified sample** divides the population into strata of similar cases, then samples
  within each stratum, usually at random;
- a **cluster sample** draws whole groups, keeping all their cases; a **multistage sample**
  draws groups and then samples within them;
- a **convenience sample** includes whoever is easy to reach, and "it is often difficult to
  discern what sub-population a convenience sample represents."

Most machine-learning datasets are convenience samples: whatever was logged, scraped or
labeled. Stratification is the one design here that is also a technique.

{{< include ../includes/cards/stratified-sampling.md >}}

On T1, with four strata cut at the quartiles of $z_1$ and samples of 200, a proportionally
allocated stratified sample estimates the mean of $\log y$ with 0.61 times the variance of a
simple random sample. The prediction $\sum_h W_h S_h^2 / S^2$ is 0.59, where $W_h$ is a
stratum's share of the population, $S_h^2$ its variance and $S^2$ the overall variance
(`tests/test_selection.py::test_stratified_sampling_lowers_the_variance_of_the_mean`).

::: {.callout-note title="In practice"}
`sklearn.model_selection.train_test_split(..., stratify=labels)` splits "in a stratified
fashion, using this as the class labels" (scikit-learn 1.9 docstring). Stratifying a split by
class keeps rare classes present in both halves. It does not make a convenience sample
representative of anything.
:::

## What it does to the learned model

Selection on $x$ changes where the model is accurate, not what it aims at. A flexible model
fit to the kept examples still targets $p(y \mid x)$, but it sees few examples where $s(x)$ is
small, so its estimate is noisy there and its errors concentrate there. A misspecified model
does worse: it chooses the best approximation *under $q(x)$*, which can be a poor approximation
where $p(x)$ puts its mass.

Selection on $y$ changes the target itself. In the demonstration, the fitted line is flatter
than the truth because large targets were removed more often where $z_1$ is large, which
pulls the high end down. The model is then miscalibrated everywhere, and the error does not
shrink with more data. It is a property of $q$, not of the sample size.

## Failure modes

![Panel A: one sample from T1; selection on $y$ keeps the colored points and drops the gray ones; the black line is the true conditional mean of $\log y$ given $z_1$ alone, and the dashed line is fit to the kept points. Panels B and C: over 200 seeds, the fitted coefficient on $z_1$ in the full regression, and the sample mean of $\log y$, for three selection rules (vertical bars are means). Selection on $x$ biases the mean but not the regression; selection on $y$ biases both.](../images/selection_bias.png){#fig-selection-bias}

@fig-selection-bias shows the two failures side by side. Three common forms:

- **Outcome-dependent recording.** Claims are filed only above a deductible; sensors saturate;
  a label is recorded only when someone complains. Each makes $s$ depend on $y$.
- **Survivorship.** The dataset contains only cases that lasted long enough to be observed,
  which again ties inclusion to the outcome.
- **Undocumented convenience.** Nobody recorded how examples were chosen, so nobody can tell
  which of the two cases applies. Datasheets were proposed against exactly this. Among the
  questions a dataset's creators answer is whether it is "a sample (not necessarily random) of
  instances from a larger set", and if so, whether it is representative
  [@gebru2018datasheets, §3.2]. A datasheet is the cheapest
  test for selection on $y$ there is.

## What the toy cannot show

T1 knows $s(x, y)$ exactly. Real selection rules are rarely written down, usually depend on
variables that are not in the dataset, and mix both cases. The demonstration also uses a
correctly specified linear model. With a misspecified model, selection on $x$ is no longer
harmless, and how much it hurts depends on the model.

## Connections

- [Labels](02-labels.qmd#sec-labels): selection on $y$ and label noise both make
  $q(y \mid x) \ne p(y \mid x)$; the next chapter treats the second.
- [Sampling and Weighting](08-sampling-and-weighting.qmd#sec-sampling): when selection depends
  on $x$ alone and $p(x)/q(x)$ is known, weighting each example by it restores the risk under
  $p$.
- [Distribution Shift](10-distribution-shift.qmd#sec-shift): the same $q \ne p$, caused by the
  world changing rather than by collection.
- [rl-for-llms, Policy Gradients](https://ioannisantoniadis.github.io/rl-for-llms/chapters/02-policy-gradients.html):
  the same pair, a sampling distribution $q$ and weights $w$, describes how reinforcement
  learning chooses its own data.
